topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on employer sample size, sectors represented, and geographic scope — these details are not evident from the title and snippet. The findings on curriculum priorities may be context-specific to particular industries or regions.
takeaways: Identify specific AI literacy gaps in your workforce by surveying employer perspectives on readiness — this reveals where training should be prioritised rather than adopting generic AI upskilling.

Align curriculum design with employer-identified priorities rather than academic assumptions about what employees need to know; the study suggests direct employer input improves workforce readiness outcomes.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European digital public health contexts; competency frameworks may have limited applicability to Australian healthcare settings or non-public-health sectors, though core AI literacy principles may transfer.
takeaways: Review identifies key competencies needed for digital public health roles in Europe; consider mapping these against your team's current capabilities to identify AI literacy gaps specific to your organisational context.

Scoping review approach means findings synthesise existing frameworks rather than present new empirical data — use as a reference for designing tailored AI upskilling programmes, not as definitive evidence of what works in practice.
Public health focus limits direct application to other sectors; if your organisation operates outside healthcare, you'll need to adapt identified competencies to your industry and workforce.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited specificity — focuses on middle school education framework development, but geographic scope and empirical validation are unclear from the snippet provided.
takeaways: AI literacy should be embedded as part of a broader digital literacy curriculum rather than taught in isolation, helping students develop interconnected competencies across multiple domains.

Middle school is a critical intervention point for building foundational AI understanding before students choose subject specialisations, making early integrated frameworks essential for equitable AI capability development.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears focused on public health faculty in higher education settings; findings may not generalise to other sectors or non-academic AI literacy programmes. Specific institutional context not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI is addressable through structured development programmes — design your AI literacy training to move people from scepticism to practical readiness rather than assuming universal buy-in from the start.
Professional development is a leverage point for scaling AI literacy — investing in training educators or subject-matter experts creates multiplier effects as they then build capability in others.
Public health context suggests domain-specific AI literacy matters — tailor your programmes to show how AI applies to your sector's real problems, not generic AI concepts.

articles.title: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting work and surveys, likely reflecting practices in large corporates and developed economies; applicability to smaller organisations or non-Western contexts unclear.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation will need foundational AI literacy versus advanced technical skills, then prioritise upskilling programmes accordingly rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach.
Design reskilling pathways for roles at risk of automation, mapping current employee capabilities to adjacent roles where AI tools will augment rather than replace human work.
Establish clear metrics for upskilling success (e.g. tool adoption rates, project completion) to track whether training translates into actual capability change and business impact.

articles.title: An epistemic-institutional artificial intelligence literacy framework for university educators - Frontiers
articles.snippet: An epistemic-institutional artificial intelligence literacy framework for university educators  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited specificity — framework is theoretically focused on university educators but geographic scope and empirical validation are unclear from the title and snippet alone. Applicability depends on institutional context and sector.
takeaways: Use an epistemic-institutional lens when designing AI literacy programmes for academic staff — integrate understanding of how AI challenges knowledge production (epistemic) with how institutional structures enable or constrain adoption.
Consider tailoring AI literacy interventions to educators' disciplinary contexts and institutional incentives, rather than delivering generic AI skills training across all departments.
Evaluate whether your organisation's policies, reward systems, and resource allocation support educators' development of meaningful AI literacy, not just technical competence.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot be fully assessed from title and snippet alone — geographic scope, sample size, and sector not indicated. Recommend checking full article for methodology details.
takeaways: AI adoption can have both positive and negative effects on employee creativity — assess whether your implementation risks deskilling or over-reliance on AI suggestions, not just efficiency gains.
Consider designing AI integration to complement rather than replace creative thinking; monitor whether teams are using AI as a creative tool or as a substitute for original problem-solving.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample composition (not detailed in snippet). Findings on paternalistic leadership may be more relevant to hierarchical organisational cultures common in some Asian contexts; applicability to flatter, more egalitarian Australian workplaces should be tested.
takeaways: Psychological ownership of AI tools—where employees feel the technology 'belongs' to them—can increase collaboration and reduce resistance; consider how onboarding and customisation practices signal ownership rather than top-down imposition.

AI crafting (tailoring AI to fit individual workflows) appears to be a mechanism linking ownership to collaboration; create space and training for employees to adapt AI tools to their specific roles rather than enforcing standardised use.

Paternalistic leadership style may moderate these effects; clarify how findings translate to Australian workplace cultures where directive, benevolent authority may be perceived differently than in contexts where paternalism is culturally normative.

articles.title: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The dual-pathway model may apply broadly to AI-enabled workforce transitions, but geographic scope, sector focus, and sample size are unclear and would affect applicability to Australian organisational contexts.
takeaways: AI transformation initiatives should address both capability development and anxiety management simultaneously — neglecting either pathway risks undermining employee engagement and job security perceptions.
Design interventions that build employee empowerment alongside AI capability training, as these appear to be distinct mechanisms affecting how workers respond to automation and technology adoption.
Monitor and assess job insecurity and anxiety as separate outcomes during AI implementation, as they may respond differently to organisational support and communication strategies.

articles.title: Worried about AI in the workplace? You’re not alone - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Worried about AI in the workplace? You’re not alone  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Limited — reflects US workforce concerns and APA membership perspectives; findings may not generalise to Australian workplace contexts with different labour market conditions, employment protections, and cultural attitudes toward technology adoption.
takeaways: Acknowledge that employee concerns about AI workplace integration are widespread and legitimate—use this validation to open dialogue rather than dismiss worries as irrational, which can improve psychological safety around the topic.

Recognise that anxiety about AI is a normal organisational change response; proactive communication about role security, skill development opportunities, and transparent implementation timelines can help reduce uncertainty-driven stress.

Consider conducting a baseline assessment of your team's specific AI-related concerns (job security, skill obsolescence, workload changes) to tailor upskilling programmes and change management strategies to actual fears rather than assumed ones.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet alone. The approach-avoidance framework may apply across sectors, but findings are likely context-dependent and require examination of actual sample composition and organisation types studied.
takeaways: Employees respond to AI adoption through distinct psychological patterns—some proactively reshape their roles (approach) while others withdraw or resist (avoidance). Understanding which pattern dominates in your workforce helps tailor adoption support.

Job crafting behaviours triggered by AI adoption can be leveraged or mitigated through targeted interventions; identify whether your organisation needs to encourage adaptive role redesign or address anxiety and disengagement that may drive avoidance responses.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology. The finding that AI adoption can negatively impact employee mental health via reduced psychological safety is important, but scope (geography, sector, sample size) cannot be assessed from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: AI implementation can increase employee depression if it erodes psychological safety — prioritise creating safe channels for employees to voice concerns about AI changes, ask questions, and report problems without fear of penalty.

Ethical leadership is a protective factor during AI adoption — leaders should explicitly communicate AI strategy, acknowledge both benefits and risks, and demonstrate commitment to fair, transparent use of AI systems.
Assess psychological safety in your team before and after AI rollout as an early warning indicator of mental health risk, not just engagement or productivity metrics.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner insights are broadly applicable across sectors, but lack empirical validation or specific geographic focus. Findings reflect Deloitte's client base, which skews toward larger organisations in developed economies.
takeaways: Shift from 'adoption' (compliance-driven) to 'adaptation' (behavioural change) messaging — frame AI initiatives around how roles evolve rather than tools being implemented, to increase buy-in and reduce resistance.

Design change interventions that explicitly target the behaviours needed for AI success (e.g. comfort with ambiguity, continuous learning, cross-functional collaboration) rather than assuming technical training alone will drive capability.
Engage frontline employees early in defining what adaptive behaviours look like in their context, rather than imposing top-down change models — this increases relevance and psychological ownership.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited without access to full methodology. The approach-avoidance framework may apply across sectors, but findings depend on sample characteristics, organisational context, and AI implementation type.
takeaways: Understand that AI adoption triggers two opposing employee responses — approach behaviours (seeking new skills, taking on AI-related tasks) and avoidance behaviours (withdrawing, resisting change) — and design interventions to reinforce approach while addressing sources of avoidance.

Use job crafting as a lever: employees who actively reshape their roles in response to AI tend to engage more constructively; encourage role redesign conversations and skill-development opportunities rather than passive acceptance of AI tools.

Assess your employees' baseline confidence and anxiety about AI before rollout; those with avoidance tendencies need early reassurance about job security and clear pathways to capability-building to shift toward approach-oriented job crafting.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reflects BCG's advisory perspective based on client engagements, likely skewed toward large multinational organisations in developed economies. Limited detail on sample composition or methodology restricts broader application.
takeaways: Reframe AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge rather than purely a technology implementation—prioritise identifying skill gaps and designing targeted upskilling pathways before deploying new tools.

Build change management into AI rollouts from the start: address employee anxiety about role displacement, involve frontline staff in design decisions, and communicate clearly how AI will augment rather than replace specific job functions.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across sectors, but specific implementation details may vary by organisational context, industry, and geography.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling not as a standalone training initiative but as a critical organisational change programme requiring executive sponsorship, clear communication of business rationale, and integration with broader strategic goals.

Design change management alongside capability building: address resistance, clarify role impacts, and establish feedback loops so employees understand how AI skills align with their career progression and organisational priorities.

Establish accountability and reinforcement mechanisms — link AI capability development to performance metrics, peer learning communities, and leadership modelling to ensure sustained behaviour change rather than one-off training attendance.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — a commentary from a US business school perspective without clear empirical grounding or geographic scope specification. Insights may reflect US labour market conditions and may not fully apply to Australian workplace contexts.
takeaways: Identify specific roles and workflows in your organisation where AI adoption is most feasible, rather than assuming uniform transformation across all teams.
Develop change management strategies that address employee concerns about AI's impact on their roles — resistance often stems from uncertainty about job security and skill relevance.
Create clear communication about how AI tools will augment rather than replace existing work, to build employee buy-in during transition periods.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited specificity from snippet alone, but findings on psychological safety and ethical leadership as mediators between AI adoption and employee wellbeing should generalise across organisations implementing AI, provided cultural and leadership contexts are comparable.
takeaways: When rolling out AI adoption, proactively establish psychological safety first — employees who feel unsafe voicing concerns about AI are more vulnerable to depression; prioritise open dialogue about fears and uncertainties.

Ethical leadership during AI transitions is protective for mental health — leaders must model and enforce clear ethical guidelines around AI use, transparency about AI impacts on roles, and genuine concern for employee wellbeing, not just efficiency gains.

Screen for depression and psychological distress in teams undergoing rapid AI adoption, particularly among employees who report low psychological safety; consider pre-adoption surveys and mental health support as part of your change strategy.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected - Science Daily
articles.snippet: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — depends on sample size, methodology, and whether findings replicate across populations.
takeaways: Scientists thought psychopathic individuals would use distinctive language patterns, but the research challenges that assumption — suggesting our stereotypes about how psychopaths 'talk' may be more Hollywood than reality.

The finding is counterintuitive: if psychopaths don't have a detectable linguistic 'tells,' it complicates both forensic assessment and everyday social detection, raising questions about how well we can spot manipulative or harmful people through conversation alone.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: High — synthesises established psychological research on friendship and health outcomes across diverse populations, though specific health mechanisms may vary by cultural context.
takeaways: Strong friendships have measurable physiological benefits — close social bonds can lower blood pressure, reduce inflammation, and boost immune function as reliably as lifestyle factors like exercise and diet.
The quality of friendships matters far more than quantity; a few deeply meaningful connections provide greater health protection than a large network of shallow relationships.

Social connection acts as a buffer against stress and mortality risk — people with strong friendships have lower rates of anxiety, depression, and premature death, rivalling the impact of quitting smoking.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Broad conceptual overview — synthesizes psychological research on true crime appeal, but specific empirical scope and geographic coverage unclear from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: True crime consumption taps into deep psychological drives: people are drawn to narratives about danger and transgression partly because they satisfy curiosity about dark human behaviour in a safe, controlled way.

The paradox of enjoyment — we find disturbing content compelling because it activates threat-detection systems while maintaining psychological distance, allowing us to explore 'the dark' without real danger.
True crime fandom reveals why humans are fascinated by rule-breaking and moral boundaries: these stories let us vicariously experience transgression and justice without personal risk.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — appears to draw on large-scale cross-cultural data, though specific sample composition not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: Your taste in music may be a surprisingly reliable window into your personality — suggesting personality traits transcend cultural boundaries in how they express themselves musically.
The finding challenges the idea that music preferences are purely culturally determined; instead, personality-driven patterns seem to hold up across different countries and regions.

This hints at something deeper about human nature: the same psychological traits that shape who you are might lead you to seek out similar sonic experiences, whether you're in Cambridge, Cairo, or Tokyo.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reviews existing research on MBTI's predictive validity, but findings are constrained by the quality and diversity of underlying studies on leadership outcomes.
takeaways: Despite MBTI's massive popularity in corporate training and leadership development, the science suggests it's surprisingly weak at actually predicting who makes a good leader — a gap between hype and evidence many organisations don't realise.

The 16 personality types feel intuitively satisfying because they're memorable and flattering, but that appeal doesn't translate into real predictive power for leadership behaviours, making it an interesting case study in why we love personality boxes even when they don't deliver.

This highlights a broader human tendency to prefer simple, elegant personality frameworks over messier but more accurate predictors — we'd rather have a type than admit leadership is genuinely complicated.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Limited — news report summarising research findings without sufficient methodological detail to assess robustness, sample size, or replicability.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies consistently find structural and functional differences in the prefrontal cortex and amygdala in individuals with psychopathic traits, regions linked to emotion processing and decision-making — a finding that challenges the idea that psychopathy is purely behavioural.

The existence of neurobiological markers for psychopathy raises fascinating questions about free will, moral responsibility, and whether brain differences should influence how we approach criminal justice and treatment.

Despite intriguing brain scan findings, researchers emphasise that neuroimaging alone cannot diagnose psychopathy or predict individual behaviour — the relationship between brain structure and real-world conduct remains complex and incompletely understood.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to full article, the sample characteristics and geographic scope are unclear. Findings on psychological safety and AI adoption may vary significantly across different organizational contexts, national cultures, and industry sectors.
takeaways: AI adoption can negatively impact employee mental health when psychological safety is low; leaders must actively foster open communication and trust during AI implementation to protect wellbeing.

Ethical leadership is a critical moderator of AI adoption outcomes — organizations should ensure leaders model ethical decision-making and accountability when introducing AI, particularly around job security concerns.

Before deploying AI, assess and strengthen psychological safety through practices like psychological safety audits, transparent change communication, and clear pathways for employees to voice concerns about automation and role changes.

articles.title: Deploying AI into workplaces: What leaders need to know - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Deploying AI into workplaces: What leaders need to know  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — APA guidance reflects US workplace context and employment law; some principles (psychological safety, change management) are broadly applicable, but specific regulatory and legal references may not transfer to Australian settings.
takeaways: Leaders should proactively communicate AI deployment plans to staff, explain how roles will change, and involve employees in design decisions to maintain psychological safety during technological change.

Create clear protocols for AI use (transparency on when AI is used, what data it accesses, how decisions are made) so employees understand the system and feel they can raise concerns without fear of reprisal.

Assess and address potential biases in AI systems before deployment, as discriminatory outcomes can undermine trust and trigger concerns about fairness—particularly important in hiring, performance management, and promotion decisions.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG report likely draws on consulting experience and case studies, but specific sample size, sectors, and geographic scope are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Teams with higher psychological safety show more equitable participation across hierarchical levels and demographic groups — monitor whether quieter team members contribute ideas equally in your 1:1s and group settings.

Create explicit norms that normalize speaking up early and admitting uncertainty; leaders should model this by asking clarifying questions rather than projecting certainty, particularly in cross-functional or diverse teams where power imbalances may otherwise suppress input.

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey perspective based on client work and industry trends, but specific case examples and organisational contexts not detailed in snippet. Findings likely reflect experiences of large, multinational organisations with resources for AI implementation.
takeaways: Psychological safety directly enables 'superagency'—the confidence to experiment with AI tools and take calculated risks without fear of failure. Create explicit permission structures where staff can test AI without penalty to foster this mindset.

Empowerment requires clarifying role boundaries between human and AI decision-making. Teams need transparent guardrails about when AI recommendations should be overridden, escalated, or accepted—this reduces anxiety and strengthens trust in AI systems.

Leadership must model psychological safety around AI uncertainty. Openly discussing AI limitations, sharing learning failures, and encouraging questions signals that not knowing is acceptable, which accelerates capability development across the organisation.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad but with standard survey limitations — findings reflect PwC's sample at a single time point (2026) and may skew toward larger organisations and developed economies where PwC operates. Results describe sentiment but causation cannot be inferred.
takeaways: Identify which workforce fears are most prevalent in your sector and organisation size to prioritise psychological safety interventions where employees feel most threatened or uncertain.

Use the survey's global data to benchmark your own team's hopes and fears against peer organisations, helping diagnose gaps in trust, transparency, or leadership communication that undermine psychological safety.
Compare regional differences in hopes and fears to tailor your safety culture messaging — what builds confidence in one market may need different emphasis elsewhere.

articles.title: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty - MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.snippet: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty  MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — theoretical perspective from a leading business school publication, applicable across sectors and geographies, though no empirical evidence or case studies are detailed in the snippet.
takeaways: Create explicit norms where team members can voice dissenting views and challenge assumptions without fear of retaliation or status loss—this directly supports psychological safety and unlocks innovative problem-solving.

Establish feedback mechanisms (e.g. anonymous channels, structured reflection sessions) that encourage people to surface doubts and alternative perspectives early in innovation projects, before ideas become entrenched.

Model intellectual honesty as a leader by publicly acknowledging uncertainty, admitting mistakes, and rewarding team members who point out flaws in proposals—this signals that honest disagreement is valued over consensus.
